original.title: Workplace culture and team climate
signals: Participation, candor, or equitable people practices on a team
A supervisor preparing a climate conversation
original.startingCompetence: You have noticed a concern with participation or team climate and want practical ways to improve everyday team practices.
original.graduatedLooksLike: By the end, you will have a team climate plan with observable practices, clear responsibilities, and a follow-up date. Complaints, investigations, and discipline continue through the appropriate formal channels.
askStarters: People on my team do not speak up in meetings. What practices could change that?
How do I write team norms that people will actually use?
Where is the line between a climate plan and an HR matter?
needsWork: A one-time conversation with no follow-up
Using the plan to investigate a named person
readyToUse: Observable practices, responsible people, and a follow-up date
Complaint concerns are directed to the appropriate formal channel
original.privacy: Please do not include names, complaint details, or discipline information. Teams are not ranked. Your progress is saved only on this computer.
original.step0Guidance: Ask about participation and team climate. Consider which everyday practices your team can change. Complaints and concerns about a named person’s conduct belong in the appropriate formal channel.
original.step1Guidance: Use a community brief only when intercultural context is directly relevant to the team's work.
original.step2Guidance: Review the team climate basics and use the action plan template.
original.step3Title: Draft your team climate action plan
original.step3Guidance: Describe the practices, participation agreements, responsible people, and a follow-up date. Please leave out names and complaint details.
original.step4Guidance: Confirm that the practices are observable, each one has a responsible person and date, and the plan contains no complaint details.
original.step5Title: Find the right person when needed
original.step5Guidance: For help preparing a team conversation, find the responsible supervisor or equity lead. Complaints and investigations belong with Employee Culture, Human Resources, or the civil-rights channel.
original.artifactField0Help: Use the team or unit name, not the names of individual people.
original.artifactField1Help: Describe something a team member could see happening in everyday work.
original.artifactField2Help: Captions on every time, materials in advance, flexible participation formats.
original.artifactField3Help: Include team input and the Equity Director when relevant, without naming anyone as the problem.
original.artifactField4Label: What you chose not to assume
original.artifactField4Help: Consider what you may not know about why people are quiet, absent, or disengaged.
original.artifactField5Label: Who is responsible for each practice
original.artifactField5Help: Name a responsible person for each practice.
original.artifactField7Help: If a workgroup will carry this work, describe its purpose and limits, how people can participate accessibly, whose perspectives are missing, and which decisions it can recommend or make under existing authority. Identify the responsible role, how participants will hear what happened to their input, and when the group will review its scope and usefulness. Do not treat joining a group as consent to speak for a community or authorize a change.
original.artifactField8Label: Expertise brief: the question and knowledge needed
original.artifactField8Help: If additional expertise would help, describe the question, what staff and affected participants already know, and which knowledge or skill is missing. Consider relevant internal expertise first. State why additional help is needed without claiming that a particular person or vendor is qualified.
original.artifactField9Label: Expertise brief: scope, deliverables and responsibility
original.artifactField9Help: Describe the proposed contribution, practical deliverables, boundaries and accountable internal role. Distinguish advice from an authorized decision. Identify how professional credentials or experience, source quality and conflicting interests would be checked by the responsible office before relying on the work.
original.artifactField10Label: Expertise brief: access, permission and review
original.artifactField10Help: Consider accessibility, language and cultural needs, time and cost, sourcing or procurement requirements, privacy and permission to share information. Record approvals as pending unless verified. Plan how the contribution will be evaluated, how affected people will hear what was used or could not be used and why, and how questions will return for review. Use the responsible program, procurement, legal, human-resources or accessibility office as applicable; this brief does not select a provider or authorize spending.
original.artifactField11Label: How the team will know the practice is helping
original.artifactField11Help: Look for changes in the team's experience without ranking or scoring people.

original.title: Planning a learning or facilitation session
signals: A training, huddle, or equity-at-work session you are running
A session that must produce application, not attendance
original.startingCompetence: You have a session to lead and want participants to leave with something they can use in their work.
original.graduatedLooksLike: By the end, you will have a reusable session plan with a clear objective, an activity based on real work, something useful participants can take with them, and access arrangements made in advance.
askStarters: How do I plan a 60-minute session that produces something participants use?
What access arrangements should be in place before a session?
What should participants leave with that they can use in their work?
needsWork: No useful work for participants to take with them
Controls or directions shown only with icons
readyToUse: A clear objective, practice with real work, and notes on assistive technology and plain language
original.privacy: Do not record or score individual participants' beliefs. If you gather feedback, report only combined results that cannot identify anyone.
original.step0Title: Begin with what participants will use
original.step0Guidance: Ask about learning and facilitation. Identify what participants should understand or practice, then record how the session will help them use it.
original.step1Guidance: If the session centers Minnesota communities, use the relevant brief with care and stay within its stated limits.
original.step2Guidance: Use the session plan template, facilitation learning guide, and access checklist as needed.

step2Links.label: Facilitation that leads to practical use

original.step3Guidance: Include the objective, activity, work participants will complete, accessibility arrangements, and follow-up.
original.step4Guidance: Confirm that participants will leave with something useful, the access arrangements are specific, and the follow-up has a date.
original.step5Title: Find the right person when needed
original.step5Guidance: If another person should help you plan the session, use Find the right person to identify the responsible role or office.
original.artifactField1Help: When using an outside course or facilitator, examine the subject and intended audience, relevant expertise and evidence, and fit with this piece of work. Confirm accessibility, participation formats, time and costs through the responsible process. Plan how participants can apply the learning and later assess whether it helped; attendance alone is not evidence of an equitable result. Leave this blank when no external learning is involved.
original.artifactField4Label: Useful work participants will leave with
original.artifactField4Help: Describe what they will complete and how they will use it next.
original.artifactField5Help: Consider captions or CART, materials shared in advance, alternatives to dragging or timed activities, plain-language slides, and text labels for every control.
original.artifactField6Label: Who helped shape or will co-facilitate
original.artifactField7Label: What you chose not to assume about participants
original.artifactField7Help: Note what you still need to learn about participants' needs and experience.
original.artifactField8Help: Name who will learn whether participants were able to use what they completed.

original.title: Inclusive hiring and selection
original.staffLabel: I'm hiring or designing a role
signals: A position description being written or revised
A hiring panel, rubric, or interview plan
A screening process that keeps producing the same result
original.startingCompetence: You are responsible for a hiring process and want it to find capable people the current process may be screening out.
original.graduatedLooksLike: By the end, you will have an inclusive hiring plan for a specific position: job-related requirements with alternatives, accessible outreach, a structured rubric and interviews, accommodation offered to everyone, a bias check built into deliberation, and a plan to review stage-by-stage outcomes with your HR partner.
askStarters: We are rewriting a position description. How do we test whether the degree requirement is really job related?
What should be in our interview rubric so we are not relying on culture fit?
How do we offer accommodation at every stage without making anyone disclose a disability?
needsWork: A diversity statement added to an unchanged posting
Removing every qualification without testing what the work requires
A panel chosen for appearance and given no rubric
readyToUse: Each requirement is tied to the work with an alternative named
The rubric is written and used
Outcomes will be reviewed stage by stage with HR
original.privacy: Do not include candidate or employee names. Describe the process, not a person. Your progress is saved only on this computer and is not used to rank anyone.
original.step0Guidance: Ask about hiring guidance and check the sources it gives you. In the hiring plan below, record the position’s relevant requirements, evaluation criteria, and outreach choices. Your HR partner confirms applicable hiring requirements.
original.step1Guidance: If outreach names particular Minnesota communities, read the relevant brief for how to reach people and what not to assume.
original.step2Guidance: Use the eight-stage lifecycle, the job-relatedness check, and the accessible meeting guidance for interviews.
original.step3Guidance: Complete the plan for this position. Your notes are saved only on this computer. Leave out candidate and employee names.
original.step4Guidance: Confirm that each requirement is tied to the work, accommodation is offered to everyone, the rubric is written, the panel is prepared, and outcomes will be reviewed with HR.
original.step5Title: Take it to the right people
original.step5Guidance: Bring the plan to your HR partner and hiring panel. Use existing workplace contacts when another professional perspective would help.
original.artifactField1Label: Requirements and what work each one predicts
original.artifactField1Help: One line per requirement: the requirement, the work it predicts, and the credible alternative that shows the same ability.
original.artifactField2Label: Where and how you will reach people outside your usual networks
original.artifactField2Help: Include community partners, plain-language posting, visible salary range, and the accommodation statement.
original.artifactField3Help: The written criteria applied the same way to every candidate. Replace culture fit with specific behaviors the team needs.
original.artifactField4Label: Accommodation and access at each stage
original.artifactField4Help: How accommodation is offered to everyone, and how each stage is accessible without disclosure.

original.artifactField5Help: Who is on the panel, how they were prepared, and which partners reviewed the plan.

original.artifactField6Help: About candidates' paths, communication styles, or what confidence looks like.

original.artifactField8Help: When you will look at who applied, advanced, and was hired.

original.title: Equity analysis for a decision
original.staffLabel: I'm making or shaping a decision that needs an equity look
signals: A policy or program change going to leadership
A budget, rule, or service decision with real reach
A decision the DHS equity policy may require an analysis for
original.startingCompetence: You own or shape a decision and want to build equity into it while it can still change, and to know whether an equity scan or a full analysis is required.
original.graduatedLooksLike: By the end, you will have an equity analysis record for a specific decision: the decision and its deadline, affected people and who is missing, evidence and its limits, benefits and burdens, alternatives, engagement, implementation owners, and follow-up. It supports the DHS process; the official record lives with the policy owner.
askStarters: We are changing a program rule that goes to leadership. Does this need an equity scan or a full analysis, and what goes in it?
Who benefits and who carries the burden in a budget reduction, and how do we find out?
What alternatives should we compare before we settle a service change?
needsWork: An equity section written after the decision was made
A single option presented as the analysis
readyToUse: The decision is stated with its real deadline
At least two alternatives are compared on benefits and burdens
Owners, follow-up, and report-back are dated
original.privacy: Do not include names or case details. This record supports a required DHS process but is not the official record; keep the official copy where your division keeps decision records. Your progress here is saved only on this computer.

original.step1Guidance: If the decision affects particular Minnesota communities, read the relevant briefs and plan engagement while the decision is open.

original.step5Title: Take it to the right people
